On Monday morning, in the nurses' room, Jonas and Mara have coffee before the shift handover. Jonas wants to know how Mara's weekend was.
Morning, Mara! So, how was the weekend? What did you do?
It was great! On Saturday I went to Potsdam with Lena.
Potsdam! Did you visit Sanssouci Palace?
Yes, of course. We walked around the park for hours. I took a hundred photos!
And the weather? Did it rain?
No, the sun was shining. In the afternoon we met Sabine, Lena's mum. She lives in Potsdam.
Then we had coffee at her place and ate cake. She showed us photos of Ludwig as a young man. He had long hair!
Mr Brandt with long hair? I want to see that! And on Sunday?
On Sunday I stayed at home. I slept a lot, called my mum and did the washing. And you?
I went to the Wannsee with Clara. We even went swimming!
In October? Are you crazy? The water is freezing!
Yes, twelve degrees. I got out after two minutes. Clara stayed in for twenty minutes. She's from Kiel, the Baltic Sea is even colder!
The participle prefix “ge-” is short and unstressed: ge-MACHT, ge-FAH-ren. The stress stays on the stem.
Watch the difference: geschrieben (“geh-SHREE-ben”), geblieben, but geschienen has a long “ie” after “sch”.
gegessen (short vowel + ss) vs. gegrüßt (long vowel + ß).
“Wannsee” = “VAN-zay”, with a long “e” at the end.

In spoken German, the past is almost always told with the Perfekt (it looks like the English present perfect “I have done”, but it's also used where English says “I did”). It's formed with HABEN or SEIN, conjugated, in position 2 + the participle at the END of the sentence:
It's the same “bracket” as with separable and modal verbs: one part of the verb in position 2, the other at the end.
2. The participle of regular verbs: ge-…-t
SEPARABLE verbs put “ge” between the prefix and the stem: einkaufen → eingekauft, anrufen → angerufen, aufstehen → aufgestanden.

Tip: learn irregular verbs in threes, with the auxiliary: “gehen – ging – ist gegangen”. You'll learn the middle form (Präteritum) at A2.
Most verbs use HABEN. SEIN is used with:
movement from one place to another
fahren, gehen, kommen, fliegen, laufen, schwimmen
sein (ist gewesen), bleiben (ist geblieben), passieren (ist passiert)
I slept a lot. (not movement → haben)
In English you say “I have gone / I have driven”, so the temptation is “Ich habe gefahren”. Wrong! With verbs of movement: “Ich BIN gefahren”.
For “to be” and “to have”, Germans prefer the short form (Präteritum) when speaking: “Es war toll” (it was great), “Ich hatte keine Zeit” (I didn't have time).

Wohin ist Mara am Samstag gefahren?

On Monday evening, Mara knocks on Ludwig's door. She has a photo on her phone: Ludwig with long hair and a guitar, in front of the tram. Sabine sent it to her in Potsdam.
Ludwig, who's this handsome young man with the guitar?
Ludwig laughs and blushes a little. Then he makes tea, sits down under his yellow tram lamp and tells his story.
That was in 1971. I was twenty-two. I was born in Prenzlauer Berg and I've always lived here. At sixteen I started at the transport company. First I repaired trams, then I became a tram driver.
And the guitar? Ah, I had a band. “The Rails”. We played in cellars and inner courtyards. Rock ’n’ roll wasn't very welcome in the GDR, you know.

At a concert I met Ingrid. She wasn't dancing. She was standing right at the back reading a book. At a rock concert! After the concert I asked her: “Didn't you like the music?” She said: “Yes, I did. But the book is better.”
Mara laughs. Fritz comes over and rests his head on Ludwig's foot.

The next day she rode on my tram. Coincidence? No! She told me later: she waited at the stop for three days. Three days! We got married in 1974. We never travelled far. Once to the Baltic Sea, once to Prague, once to Hungary, to Lake Balaton. But we were very happy.
And in 1989? What was it like when the Wall came down?

On the ninth of November I was on the late shift. At midnight, suddenly, hundreds of people got on my tram. They all wanted to go to Bornholmer Straße, to the border. They were laughing, singing, crying. A woman hugged me, in the middle of the route! I stopped the tram and got off too. I crossed the border on foot, in my uniform. On the other side a man gave me a beer. I didn't drink it. I was on duty, after all!
Ludwig is silent for a while. Then he gets up, goes to the wardrobe and takes out an old guitar. Three strings are missing.
Ingrid died five years ago. I haven't played since.

Mara says nothing. But the next day, after work, she goes to a music shop on Schönhauser Allee and buys six new guitar strings. She leaves them in a little parcel outside Ludwig's door, with a note: “For “The Rails”. Your neighbour from the third floor.”
In the evening, the whole house hears something new: beneath Mrs Hoffmann's piano, very softly, a guitar is playing.
Was hat Ingrid auf dem Konzert gemacht?
Was hat Ludwig am 9. November gemacht?
Er ist zu Fuß über die Grenze gegangen.
